strengths: Clear and compelling motivation with excellent visual examples (Figure 1) demonstrating LLM sampling bias and how partitioning mitigates it
Sound algorithmic design combining KD-tree partitioning, principled UCB-V based scoring, and LLM sampling with proper connection to bandit theory
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple problem domains (synthetic functions, HPO, NAS) with strong baselines (BO variants, evolutionary methods) and proper ablations
Excellent reproducibility with detailed pseudocode, algorithm details, experimental setup, and prompts; code repository provided
Good visualizations of algorithm mechanics (Figures 2, 4, 8) showing how partitions adaptively refine during optimization
Consistent improvements over global LLM baseline and competitive or superior performance compared to established methods like TuRBO on several benchmarks
Thoughtful design choices (e.g., empirical maximum for exploitation to handle heteroscedasticity, geometric volume for dimension-invariant exploration)
Multiple random seeds with error bars and extended ablations examining hyperparameter sensitivity
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (KD-tree partitioning from HOO, UCB-V from bandit literature) with LLM sampling; no new algorithmic insights or theoretical contributions

Lack of theoretical guarantees: no regret bounds or convergence analysis; re-fitting KD-tree at every iteration breaks standard bandit theory; no formal analysis of how LLM proposal quality affects optimization

Experimental concerns: only 6 synthetic benchmarks with 100 iterations; improvements often modest (e.g., Rosenbrock); inconsistent results (underperforms on Parkinsons); weak global LLM baseline; missing comparisons with recent LLM-based BO methods [34,60,64]; only 3 runs for synthetic benchmarks

Many arbitrary design choices with limited justification: specific UCB-V formulation, d-th root for volume, max over mean for exploitation, default variance (0.01) for small samples, cosine annealing schedule; min-max normalization crucial but under-analyzed

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity revealed in ablations: optimal αmax is task-dependent (Figure 10); sensitivity to m₀, k, M (Figure 9) suggests problem-specific tuning required; many tuning knobs limit practical applicability

Scalability limitations: largest experiment only 20D (Ackley); no evaluation beyond 20 dimensions; unclear scalability to truly high-dimensional problems; O(t log t) KD-tree construction plus LLM inference costs

Heavy LLM dependency: method success depends on LLM proposal quality; no analysis of LLM calibration or miscalibration effects; only Gemini-1.5-Flash tested as primary LLM; no systematic comparison across LLM families
Ablation results (Figure 7) show LLM choice dominates; comparison with KDTree+GP suggests partitioning alone provides limited additional benefit beyond using any partitioning strategy
Incomplete analysis: inconsistent results on Parkinsons task not well explained; no statistical significance testing; LLM inference costs not discussed compared to traditional BO

strengths: Clear and compelling motivation with effective demonstrations of LLM sampling bias (Figure 1) that justify the core approach
Well-designed composite scoring function (Eq. 3) that elegantly balances exploitation, geometric exploration, and uncertainty quantification with principled normalization

Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (synthetic optimization, hyperparameter tuning, NAS) showing consistent improvements over global LLM baseline and competitiveness with state-of-the-art methods like TuRBO/BORE/CQR
Thorough ablation studies (Figures 7-9) clearly identifying the value of each component and demonstrating robustness of design choices
Strong empirical results on high-dimensional multimodal problems (e.g., Ackley-20D solved efficiently) demonstrating practical utility
High reproducibility: detailed pseudocode, complete hyperparameters, full prompts, and promised code release enabling verification and adoption
Honest treatment of limitations and clear writing with helpful visualizations of algorithm dynamics
weaknesses: No theoretical analysis or regret guarantees; gap between infinite-armed bandit framing and actual dynamic KD-tree algorithm is not addressed, limiting theoretical understanding

Limited novelty in individual components—KD-tree partitioning, UCB-V exploration, and hypervolume-based search are all established techniques; main contribution is their combination, which while sensible is somewhat incremental

LLM quality and calibration largely unexamined: only Gemini-1.5-Flash tested, no analysis of output calibration or when LLM-based generation fails; Parkinsons dataset (Figure 5) shows global LLM outperforming HOLLM without clear explanation

Scalability not thoroughly demonstrated: largest tested dimension is 20D; no high-dimensional experiments (50D+) where partitioning efficiency matters most, and no computational cost comparisons with baselines

Hyperparameter sensitivity and tuning requirements: many hyperparameters with task-dependent optimal settings (e.g., α_max in Figure 10), suggesting real-world deployment may require problem-specific tuning

Limited experimental scope: only 100 iterations with three runs per condition and no error bars on main results; missing comparisons with other recent LLM-based optimization methods beyond global baseline
Marginal improvements in some cases (FCNet results often within error margins) and inconsistent performance (Parkinsons underperformance) raise questions about robustness across problem types

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 1) showing LLM sampling bias and how partitioning improves spatial coverage via Hausdorff distance analysis
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmark categories (6 synthetic functions, 4 HPO datasets, 3 real-world tasks, NAS) with strong baselines including TurBO and LA-MCTS
Thoughtfully designed composite scoring function (Eq. 3) balancing exploitation, geometric exploration, and statistical exploration via UCB-V, with principled annealing and normalization
Consistent strong empirical results outperforming baselines on most tasks, particularly multimodal functions; best average rank via critical difference diagram
Extensive analysis beyond basic results: sample diversity via ICL Divergence, surrogate calibration comparison with GPs/TabPFN, computational complexity showing O(t²) vs O(t³) advantage
Robustness to LLM model choice demonstrated across Gemini, Llama, and Qwen models with detailed ablations in appendices
Thorough reproducibility considerations with detailed pseudocode, prompt templates, and promise of code release; ethical reflection on biases and societal impact
weaknesses: Limited theoretical insight: no formal regret bounds or convergence guarantees; connection to bandit theory (HOO, UCB-AIR) is motivational rather than rigorous, leaving performance limits unclear

Limited technical novelty: primarily integrates existing components (KD-trees from HOO/TurBO, UCB-V from Audibert et al. 2009, straightforward LLM application) without fundamental new insights; engineering-focused rather than research-focused contribution

Insufficient high-dimensional evaluation: most benchmarks ≤10D; Ackley-20D results relegated to appendix; Rastrigin-10D underperforms baselines with insufficient analysis of why partitioning hurts on highly multimodal separable functions

Heavy hyperparameter tuning requirements: many hyperparameters (m₀, λ, αmax, αmin, β₁, β₂, M, k, b); ablations show significant sensitivity (Figure 13-14); αmax is task-dependent; no principled selection method provided

Significant performance degradation on discrete spaces: explicitly acknowledged that FCNet benefits are 'less pronounced' due to discrete nature; only ordinal encoding applied without specialized categorical handling, limiting applicability to important HPO domain

Limited comparison to alternative LLM-based optimization methods: only compares to own global LLM baseline (Algorithm 2) rather than recently published methods (Liu et al. 2024, Agarwal et al. 2025, Song et al. 2024); cannot isolate contribution of partitioning

Heavy dependence on LLM quality with insufficient mechanistic understanding: global baseline fails completely with Llama-3.1-8B but HOLLM succeeds (Figure 8a) without clear explanation; LLM ranking correlation of τ≈0.76 leaves 24% ranking error unaddressed

Missing statistical significance testing: results show mean ± std error without hypothesis tests; several differences have overlapping error bars (e.g., Figure 5 Hartmann functions); cannot verify if improvements are statistically significant

Discrete prompt engineering contradicts 'minimal task information' claim: dynamic constraints, global in-context examples, structured instructions, and task-specific templates (Listing 5 differs from Listing 3) require tuning; prompt sensitivity not evaluated
Incomplete noise robustness evaluation: tested only on Vehicle Safety with 1% homoscedastic noise; real-world problems often have higher or non-homoscedastic noise; generalization unclear

Actual computational cost analysis incomplete: only one data point ($0.14 for 330 seconds on Vehicle Safety); no systematic wall-clock time comparison; practitioners need actual runtime vs. function evaluations trade-off analysis

Limited real-world evaluation: all three tasks from single source (Tanabe & Ishibuchi 2020); all small (5-7D); problems may not be truly expensive; diverse real-world problems needed to strengthen claims

Use of global in-context history potentially undermines localization principle: paper justifies global history to prevent 'overfitting to local patterns' but this violates core partitioning benefit; no ablation provided comparing local-only vs. global history

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 1) that LLMs struggle with high-dimensional sampling, clearly demonstrated through Hausdorff distance analysis
Principled technical approach combining KD-tree partitioning with composite UCB-inspired scoring function that thoughtfully balances exploitation, geometric exploration, and statistical exploration
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse problem types (synthetic, HPO, NAS, real-world) with strong baselines (TuRBO, LA-MCTS, BORE, CQR, GP-EI) and consistent improvements

Exceptional supplementary analysis including systematic hyperparameter ablations, cross-LLM robustness evaluation, surrogate calibration analysis, and sample diversity metrics that provide deep insights
High reproducibility with detailed algorithms, complete prompt templates, specified hyperparameters, and runtime/cost analysis, facilitating future work and practical deployment
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 2, 4, 12) that illustrate algorithm mechanics and design choices intuitively
Honest acknowledgment of limitations including lack of theoretical guarantees, hyperparameter sensitivity, and LLM quality dependency, avoiding overclaimed contributions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: KD-tree partitioning, UCB-based scoring, and variance-aware exploration are established techniques; the main contribution is their combination with LLM sampling rather than fundamentally new ideas
Absence of theoretical guarantees: paper explicitly lacks regret bounds or theoretical analysis, making it unclear why the method works or under what problem conditions it should be preferred

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity: multiple hyperparameters (m₀, λ, αmax, αmin, β₁, β₂, M, k) show task-dependent optimal values (Figure 14), with limited guidance for practitioners beyond empirical defaults

Strong dependency on LLM quality: performance varies substantially across models (Gemini-2.0 vs. Llama-3.1-8B in Figure 8a), and global LLM baseline fails with weaker models, limiting accessibility and increasing deployment costs

Weaker performance on discrete/categorical search spaces: hyperparameter optimization results (Figure 5) show less dramatic improvements, and ceiling effects noted for certain tasks, suggesting method may not generalize across all problem types
Strong spatial partitioning baselines (TuRBO, LA-MCTS) relegated to appendix despite representing natural comparisons; main paper comparison coverage could be more thorough

Incomplete computational cost analysis: lacks wall-clock time comparisons against baselines, API latency/cost discussion is superficial, and computational efficiency claims versus GP methods are not empirically demonstrated
Sampling efficiency concerns: default settings wastefully generate k·M=25 candidates but evaluate only b=4, with no sensitivity analysis of this trade-off or impact on sample efficiency
Limited failure mode analysis: Rastrigin results notably weaker (Figure 3) without explanation; missing discussion of problem characteristics where global sampling might outperform partitioning
Modest improvements on some problem classes: hyperparameter optimization and discrete domains show smaller gains compared to continuous, moderately multimodal functions where method excels
